name: PT Soechi Lines Tbk
industry_name: Gas & fuel distribution, refining and marketing

frontmatter.title: Soechi Lines: the fleet is worth more than the earnings
frontmatter.summary: A tanker owner trading at a fraction of book. The fleet's secondhand value exceeds its carrying value, but at through-cycle freight the equity is worth about today's price: our DCF and own-history multiples sit below it, and the target leans on a one-in-five bull case. HOLD.
thesis: Fleet renewal is complete: the current year is a cyclical high on a larger, better-chartered fleet, not a new run-rate.
The anchor customer cut its nine-month spend by nearly a quarter, so concentration has crystallised rather than remaining a static risk.
Correcting tax to the final-tax mechanism and capex to a net basis lifts the DCF, but not enough to close the gap to the price.
The discount to book is the arithmetic of a mid-single-digit ROE against a high-teens cost of equity, not an anomaly to arbitrage.
Leverage near four times net debt to EBITDA makes the equity an option on freight rates; the bull case is asset value and re-rating, not earnings.
Family control, a thin float and related-party ship-management flows justify a discount that the asset value does not remove.

catalysts.event: Fourth-quarter charter renewals and full-year revenue against the company's own guidance range
Audited full-year results: the first full year of the enlarged fleet and the peak fleet-investment year
Refinancing of the acquisition facilities and the sukuk ijarah maturity profile
Tanker orderbook deliveries: the supply test for spot rates

blocks.text: Soechi Lines owns and operates one of the larger Indonesian-flag tanker fleets — 30 vessels and 1.39 million DWT at the end of FY2025 — together with a shipyard that repairs and occasionally builds vessels [S3]. It reports in US dollars, earns dollar freight from Indonesian and international charterers, and lists in Jakarta. At Rp410 the equity trades below the book value of US$438.2m reported at 30 September 2026, which for a company whose assets are ships with observable secondhand prices is the question this report has to answer [S2].

Our rating is **HOLD** with a target of **Rp439**, a total return of 9.1% [S3][S2]. The target must be read carefully, because it is a probability-weighted number and the base case is weaker: the base-case value is Rp266, below the share price, and only the bull scenario carries the blend above the market. We hold rather than sell because the asset backing is real, the shares already discount a poor return on it, and the bull case is worth several times the base case; we do not buy because nothing in the accounts says the fleet will earn its cost of capital soon, and no dated catalyst forces the value out.

The variant view is not that tanker rates stay at the current high — we fade them. It is that the market has already priced the arithmetic correctly. A tanker owner earning a mid-single-digit return on equity should trade below book when the cost of equity is in the high teens, and this one does. The mispricing, if there is one, is in the tail: the same leverage that makes the base case dull makes the bull case violent, and the fleet's secondhand value gives that tail an asset floor [S6].

What changed in this revision, and why. First, the cross-check: the previous draft let a peer EV/EBITDA median, set by two incomparable observations, carry a third of the target. It now carries a tenth of the weight on the company's own five-year history, and the peer table is shown for reference rather than used [S0]. Second, revenue: anchored to the nine-month actual and the company's own full-year guidance rather than an unsourced growth rate [S2][S3]. Third, tax: built from the final-tax mechanism on freight revenue, not a midpoint of two distorted years [S3]. Fourth, capex: net of disposal proceeds, because the company sells vessels every year and the gross line double-charged the DCF [S2]. Fifth, the balance sheet: the drawn facilities are on the debt line, so projected debt ties to the filing and interest is charged on the full balance from FY2027E [S2].

Two segments. Shipping contributed US$135.5m of FY2025 net revenue and the shipyard US$19.7m [S3], so this is a tanker company with a workshop attached, not a diversified industrial. Within shipping, revenue splits between time charter — contracted, largely fixed daily rates — and spot voyages. In the first nine months of 2026 time charter produced US$102.3m against spot US$27.1m; a year earlier the same lines were US$92.3m and US$10.4m [S2]. The contracted book is what makes a leveraged balance sheet survivable in a soft market; the spot book, which more than doubled, is what produced the current earnings jump.

The fleet is mid-age and mixed: crude and product tankers plus gas carriers, including an LNG carrier and a medium-range product tanker acquired during 2025, both placed on charter [S3]. The annual report records two vessel acquisitions in 2025, one in each half, and two disposals of older gas and oil tankers, leaving 30 tankers and 1.39 million DWT at the year-end, with average utilisation of 86.0% [S3]. The third-quarter filing does not disclose a vessel count: it shows additions to vessel cost, net of disposals, not a number of hulls [S2]. Company statements in October 2026 report two tankers added during the third quarter, one gas and one oil carrier, which is consistent with the additions in the filing. We carry their earning contribution inside the current-year revenue run-rate and therefore inside the FY2027 base, but we do not restate the year-end hull count of 30 vessels without a filing that gives one, and we say so rather than invent a number.

Customers are the Indonesian energy complex, and the mix has moved sharply. In the first nine months of 2026 Pertamina Patra Niaga took US$28.4m, above a tenth of the total, while Pertamina International Shipping fell to US$1.8m from US$38.9m in the comparable period [S2]. That is not a like-for-like switch inside one group: the two entities together accounted for about a fifth of nine-month revenue against roughly a third a year earlier, and the anchor customer spent materially less with the company rather than simply moving it [S2]. This is the most important commercial fact in the file, and it is why the customer relationship is the bear case's mechanism rather than a footnote.

The shipyard handled 37 vessels in 2025, mostly repair and dry-docking, and management has said it will be selective about newbuilding orders [S3]. Segment operating margin was negative in FY2025 [S3], so the yard is currently a cost of doing business and a source of docking capacity rather than a profit centre. It is not worthless: land, buildings and yard capacity sit on the balance sheet inside total assets of US$603.5m [S3], and we give it book value in the asset cross-check rather than an earnings value.

Strategy, as disclosed, is fleet renewal plus geographic diversification: subsidiaries were established in Indonesia, the Marshall Islands and the United Arab Emirates to pursue shipping opportunities, and the group uses sale-and-leaseback and sukuk alongside bank debt [S2][S3]. Management's stated aim is to keep utilisation high and widen the customer base beyond the domestic anchor. The fleet programme is visible in the cash flow: nine-month purchases of US$157.0m against proceeds of US$35.2m, funded by US$130.9m of bank-loan drawdowns and a sukuk issue [S2].

Competitive position: a leader in Indonesian-flag tanker tonnage, a challenger internationally [S3]. The moat is regulatory and relational — cabotage rules, national oil company relationships, a domestic yard for docking — not technological. That is real but narrow: it protects the domestic franchise and does nothing for the spot earnings that drove the current year. It also explains why the customer can cut spend without losing the ships its cargo needs: the relationship is exclusive in neither direction.

Tanker shipping is a freight-rate market with inelastic short-run supply, because ships take years to build, and demand derived from crude and product trade. Indonesian demand is structurally supported by import dependence on refined products and by domestic crude movements; global demand follows OPEC+ policy, ton-miles and the orderbook [S3]. Supply is the part that matters now. About 11.8% of the tanker fleet is on order, the crude orderbook is larger still, and newbuild values are near record levels [S7]. Secondhand values have followed: an older medium-range product tanker changed hands at US$24.5m and a suezmax at US$98.0m in recent weeks, with brokers describing the market as stabilised at a high level after a year of gains [S6].

The domestic market is the part that is not purely cyclical. Indonesian refinery capacity does not cover domestic product demand, so the country imports refined product and moves crude between islands; both flows need tankers, and cabotage reserves domestic voyages to Indonesian-flag tonnage [S3]. That is the floor under utilisation, and it is why the company has been able to place newly acquired vessels on charter rather than in the spot market [S3]. The ceiling is set globally: when international rates fall, domestic charterers reprice at renewal toward the imported alternative, so the domestic franchise moderates the cycle rather than abolishing it.

The economics are violently cyclical. A single year can move operating profit by more than the entire equity base: FY2025 operating profit was US$29.9m on revenue of US$155.3m [S3], while nine months of the current year produced US$36.2m of operating income on US$137.5m of revenue [S2]. Gross margin moved from 26.5% to 31.5% on our full-year estimate. Anyone underwriting this name must accept that the current margin is a cyclical reading, not a run-rate, and that the orderbook is the reason to fade it.

Tax and regulation shape returns more than most investors realise. Indonesian-source freight and charter income is subject to a final income tax of 1.2% of revenue, with related costs non-deductible [S3]. That is why the effective rate on reported pre-tax profit was so low in the first nine months of the current year [S2], and why a shift in revenue mix — more foreign-flag, more shipyard — changes the group tax charge without changing operating performance. The final-tax base is freight and charter revenue; shipyard revenue is taxed normally, and the accounts show both a final and a non-final charge [S2].

Oil prices reach this business through two channels, and neither is a mechanical cost link. Bunker fuel is the largest variable cost on spot voyages, but on time charter it is the charterer's cost, and the time-charter book is the majority of revenue [S2]. The oil deck has Brent at US$84.0 for FY2027E against US$91.8 spot, and Indonesian crude at US$78.0 against US$112.8 — a disinflationary path for the oil complex [S0]. For a tanker owner that is a modest bunker tailwind and a modest trade-value headwind; it is not a revenue line, because freight rates are set by vessel supply and cargo demand, not by the price of the cargo. We therefore keep the cost link switched off. That is a deliberate divergence from the covered downstream peer that runs its fuel cost against Brent: a distributor buys and resells the molecule and its margin is a spread on it, while this company sells the voyage [S2].

Market share: the company describes itself as one of the largest tanker operators in Indonesia [S3]. We cannot source an independent share estimate and we do not invent one. The relevant competitive facts are a fleet of 30 vessels, a domestic yard, cabotage protection, and an anchor customer that is also the national oil company's trading and shipping arm.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate: shipyards and secondhand sellers set the price of growth, and the current year was an expensive year to buy tonnage [S6]. Buyer power is high and concentrated, and the nine-month customer data shows it being exercised [S2]. New entrants face capital and cabotage barriers, but the secondhand market is liquid, so barriers are moderate. Substitutes are pipelines and product imports carried by others. Rivalry is global and rate-driven, with domestic rivalry muted by the anchor relationship. This is our structural read, informed by the fleet and customer disclosures.

External influences that matter: tanker spot rates and the orderbook, which we treat as the primary driver of the next two years; the rupiah, because reporting is in dollars and the IDR share price moves with the exchange rate even when the business does not; Indonesian fuel-subsidy policy, which determines how much product the national oil company moves; and dollar interest rates, because the debt is dollar-denominated and now stands at US$253.2m [S2].
Financial summary:
The historical series is the data pack [S0], restated where the filings disagree with it [S2][S3].

Revenue was US$155.3m in FY2025, below the prior year's US$165.6m [S3], then grew again: nine-month revenue reached US$137.5m [S2]. We forecast current-year revenue growth of 12.0% to US$173.9m. That is anchored to two things the company controls less than it would like: nine months are already US$137.5m, so a flat fourth quarter takes the year to roughly our number, and management guided to a range from US$160.0m [S3]. We sit above the top of that range, because a flat fourth quarter on the nine-month run-rate already exceeds it, and we say so rather than round the forecast down to the guidance; we do not extrapolate the third-quarter spot spike. Growth then decelerates to 3.0% as the fleet base stabilises and spot rates normalise.

Margins. Gross margin was 26.5% in FY2025 and 31.5% on our current-year estimate; the nine-month actual was higher still, and we trim for a yard-heavy fourth quarter [S2][S3]. The fade to 28.5% is rate normalisation, and it lands above the FY2025 actual, so the base case is not a disguised bear case. SG&A is held at 6.5% of revenue, in line with the nine-month ratio [S2].

The most important correction we make to the data pack is depreciation. The reported financials carry a depreciation charge of US$18.6m for FY2025 against US$18.4m in the prior year [S3]; the pack's own line was a small fraction of that, as it is for most IDX filings under the direct cash-flow method. We restate depreciation from the fixed-asset note for the last two fiscal years, which rebuilds EBITDA and stops us quoting a cash cost that flatters the business. Every margin and every multiple in this report depends on it.

Costs. Vessel operating expenses, docking, crewing and insurance dominate the cost of revenue [S2]. Docking is recurring and lumpy — capital maintenance by another name — and we treat it as an operating cost, not as capex to be added back. Interest is the second fixed claim: finance costs were US$10.0m in nine months, a run-rate near US$10.6m, and the charge rises to US$16.0m once the drawn balance is in place, against our contractual rate of 6.3% [S2].

Cash flow and capex. Nine-month operating cash flow was US$32.3m [S2], a healthy conversion of a US$137.5m revenue base. Gross capex was US$157.0m in the same nine months, funded by new bank loans and sukuk, and the company also realised US$35.2m from vessel disposals [S2]. The DCF must charge the net figure, because both are investing cash flows. Our capex path is therefore 81.0% of revenue in the current year — gross purchases less disposal proceeds — normalising to 18.0% and 15.0% in the long run. That is the honest treatment of a fleet that is bought and sold: the previous draft charged the gross line and ignored the sale proceeds, which understated current-year free cash flow by the disposal amount.

Balance sheet and debt. At 30 September 2026 total liabilities were US$289.7m against equity of US$438.2m [S2]. Interest-bearing debt at that date was bank loans of US$215.2m long-term including current maturities plus US$10.0m short-term, sukuk ijarah of US$7.4m, sale-and-leaseback liabilities of US$7.0m due within a year and US$13.2m beyond it, lease liabilities of US$0.2m and US$0.2m, and consumer-financing payables of US$0.0m and US$0.0m. Those are the components of the total, not additions to it: the sale-and-leaseback balance sits inside interest-bearing debt, which the previous draft got wrong. Against cash of US$10.2m, net debt at the period end was therefore close to the US$239.4m we carry at the year-end, and the US$130.9m of bank-loan proceeds drawn in the nine months is what funded the fleet programme [S2]. Our projected cash of US$13.7m is the residual after that programme, the dividend and the drawdown, and it stays positive through the forecast.

Capital allocation. The company pays a token dividend and retains the rest for fleet renewal. The stated policy is nil to 30.0% of profit attributable to owners [S3]; the actual payout was about a tenth of FY2025 earnings and less than that in nine months of the current year [S2]. That is defensible for a business with expensive equity and observable asset values, and it is also why the equity trades below book: retained cash goes into ships that earn a mid-single-digit return.

Earnings quality flags. First, the company's own EBITDA measure of US$62.9m for FY2025 [S3] is materially above EBITDA rebuilt as operating profit plus the note's depreciation charge; the difference is other add-backs we do not accept as non-recurring, and we use the rebuilt figure. Second, accruals are not a concern: nine-month operating cash flow of US$32.3m tracks profit, so earnings are converting to cash. Third, the nine-month profit and loss account carries a US$6.2m gain on disposal of fixed assets inside other income [S2]; we exclude it from recurring profit, and because the proceeds are already in investing cash flow the gain is not a second benefit. Fourth, FY2025 carried a disposal loss that depressed that year's profit and its effective tax rate [S3]. Fifth, non-controlling interests are immaterial at US$0.5m of balance-sheet equity [S2]. Sixth, the auditor is a mid-tier firm and the free float is thin; neither is a manipulation signal on its own, but both argue for a discount [S3].

Reconciling current-year profit to the nine-month actual: reported nine-month net profit was US$32.3m, including the US$6.2m disposal gain [S2]. Stripping the gain leaves a recurring nine-month run-rate below our full-year recurring forecast of US$31.3m, which carries that run-rate through a flat fourth quarter and adds the interest on the newly drawn debt. The reported full-year figure will therefore be higher than our recurring number by the gain. We model the recurring line because vessel trading is episodic in timing even when it is routine in frequency.

We use a discounted cash flow as the only valuation method, at a weight of 100.0%. Shipping is capital-intensive, asset-backed and dollar-earning; its value is the present value of freight cash flows after fleet investment, and a DCF captures the capex cycle that a single-year multiple cannot. The previous draft carried two earnings-multiple legs at ten per cent each and a dividend-yield leg at zero; all three are now removed, and the argument for the change is in the cross-check discussion below rather than buried in a weight. This is a deliberate departure from the industry default of a DCF plus two cross-checks, and we are explicit that it puts the whole target on one method.
Cost of capital:

The WACC of 9.8% is built from a dollar risk-free rate of 4.9%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.8x from the industry default because the company has no usable regression history, and a levered beta of 1.8x [S0]. Two method points need stating because the previous draft was unclear about both. First, the gearing ratio of 1.6x is gross debt over market capitalisation at today's price, not the book debt-to-equity ratio: at book, debt of US$253.2m against equity of US$438.2m is less than six-tenths of equity, and the cost of equity at that gearing would be materially lower. We use market weights because that is what a marginal investor faces, but the reader should know the choice is worth a lot. Second, the country premium sits inside the beta-scaled equity premium, so the cost of equity is 16.8%; adding it outside beta instead would give a cost of equity a couple of points lower and a proportionately higher DCF. We keep the house convention and flag it as the largest single judgement in the discount rate.

The cost of debt in the WACC is 6.9%, the dollar risk-free rate plus a corporate spread from the deck; the profit and loss account uses the contractual rate of 6.3% implied by nine-month finance costs on average drawn debt [S2]. Those are not the same number and should not be: one is the market's forward cost of new borrowing, the other is the average coupon on the existing stack. Debt is 61.2% of the capital structure, which is why the equity behaves like an option.
Primary method:

The DCF values the equity at Rp234, below the market price, with terminal value at 58.9% of enterprise value. That share is the DCF's main weakness and we state it plainly: more than half of the value comes from a perpetuity, so the method is only as good as the long-run margin and growth assumptions, not the ten explicit years. Read the rest honestly too. The DCF charges the current-year fleet programme net of disposal proceeds, assumes replacement capex of 15.0% of revenue against depreciation of 11.0%, and discounts at a cost of capital built on market gearing. It is not a liquidation value: the enterprise value of US$335.3m sits well above the net book value of the vessels at US$132.0m, because a going concern earns a return on hulls that are largely depreciated, and below their gross cost of US$414.2m [S2]. That tells you the DCF is capitalising earnings, not assets. If the ships are worth what the secondhand market says, the DCF is too low; if they are not, the market price is too high.
Cross-checks:

The table carries the primary method alone, and the reason is arithmetic, not tactical. The EV/EBITDA leg the previous draft weighted at ten per cent took its multiple from the data pack's own five-year EV/EBITDA history. That history divides enterprise value by pack EBITDA, and pack EBITDA uses a depreciation charge that is a fraction of the US$18.6m the fixed-asset note reports for FY2025 [S0][S3] — the same restatement this report makes everywhere else. Dividing the same enterprise values by a much smaller denominator inflates every year's multiple; on the restated EBITDA series the four observations average about six times against the pack's nearly nine. The engine gives us no way to feed it a rebuilt history, so the honest response is to remove the weight rather than keep a leg we know is overstated by roughly a third. On a trough-year denominator that would have been the largest single error in the target, and it would have pointed the wrong way.

The second leg, on P/E, goes with it for the same reason: it is built on the same stale pack earnings, and its latest observation is distorted by the FY2025 disposal loss. We keep both in the discussion because the reader is entitled to see what they implied — they produced a value well above the DCF, and a target that leaned on them would have said the shares are cheap on numbers this report has just spent a page correcting.
The peer evidence, shown for reference and deliberately not weighted:

The four names in that table are the Indonesian tanker and shipping owners the pack tracks, with each name's LTM multiple and the pack's EBITDA definition [S0]. Every figure in it is a trailing number, which is the honest label but also the problem: for this company the trailing comparison would use nine-month 2026 operating income of US$36.2m against US$29.9m for the whole of FY2025 [S2][S3], and the pack's own LTM series has not caught up with that step-up. The set is also dispersed enough that the median describes none of the four: a small-cap quoted at a deep discount to the others, and three carrying multiples that reflect their own charters and leverage rather than a sector rule. The gas-infrastructure, gas-distribution and fuel-distribution names a generic Indonesia screen would add are a different business, one of them carrying a conglomerate premium this firm treats with suspicion and one with LTM EBITDA close enough to zero that its ratio is an artefact. That dispersion is why neither a peer median, nor a single-year multiple of our own history, carries weight in the target.

A net asset value check, because the balance sheet is the other side of this story. The vessels are carried at US$132.0m net of depreciation against a gross cost of US$414.2m at the end of the prior year [S2]. The company's own realised prices are the best available mark: it sold two vessels in FY2025 for US$31.5m, against a carrying value of US$37.5m, a loss of the difference [S3]. Extending that realised price per hull across the fleet gives a value of roughly fifteen times those proceeds — before any credit for the newer LNG and medium-range units acquired in 2025, and before the land and yard inside total assets of US$603.5m. Add those, subtract the US$253.2m of debt, and net asset value is a large multiple of the current market capitalisation. We do not put it in the target, for a reason that is itself the investment case: a fleet worth more than its book only pays out if it is sold, and there is no disclosed sale process, no dividend policy that returns the value, and a controlling family that has chosen to reinvest. The wide range — from scrap value for the oldest hulls to the recent medium-range mark of US$24.5m — is why we treat net asset value as a bull-case anchor rather than a valuation.

What the price implies: at Rp410 the market requires FY2027E revenue growth of 8.6% against our 6.0% [S0]. The market is therefore not assuming a collapse in freight; it is assuming slightly more growth than we do, on a stock at a fraction of book. That is a market that believes the earnings, not the assets. Our target of Rp439 is a 9.1% total return and requires the enlarged fleet to earn a normal shipping return on a normalised margin, with the bull tail doing most of the work.

The book anchor deserves the arithmetic rather than an assertion. On our forecasts the return on equity is 7.4%, the cost of equity is 16.8% and terminal growth is 2.0%; a justified price-to-book is the return spread over the discount-rate spread, which on those inputs is a discount to book close to the one the market applies at 0.4x. The discount is therefore the arithmetic of a low return on equity, not an anomaly, and book is not an anchor independent of the forecasts. The target sits at roughly half of book value per share, which by the same arithmetic requires a return on equity around the midpoint between our terminal growth rate and our cost of equity — a recovery in returns, not a re-rating of the same returns.

An AFFO and FCFE check, because the method card asks for a cash yield against the ten-year rate. AFFO is EBITDA of US$64.5m less maintenance capex — for which we use the depreciation charge of US$21.2m as the standing proxy for steel renewal and docking — less cash interest of US$16.0m and cash tax of US$1.5m. Because the maintenance charge offsets depreciation, AFFO per share converges on EPS, so the AFFO yield is the reciprocal of the 6.2x P/E at Rp410; the whole spread over the 4.9% ten-year dollar rate is the compensation for 3.7x turns of net debt and spot-linked earnings, and it is a spread on an equity that the bear case shows can be wiped out. FCFE is negative while the fleet programme runs, -4.5% in the current year, and turns positive in FY2028E at 4.5%. The dividend-yield leg is not used at all: the stated policy is nil to 30.0% of attributable profit [S3] and the actual payout is a token amount, so a yield valuation would measure management's retention choice rather than the value of the equity, and it would collapse toward zero by construction.
Sensitivity:
Principal risks, with likelihood and impact:

items: **Freight-rate reversal (high likelihood, high impact).** About 11.8% of the tanker fleet is on order and rising, and spot revenue more than doubled [S2][S7]. A return to prior-year conditions takes operating profit back toward US$29.9m [S3] and coverage thins.

**Anchor-customer concentration (high, high).** The two national oil company entities together fell from about a third of revenue to about a fifth in nine months, with Pertamina International Shipping down to US$1.8m from US$38.9m [S2]. If the anchor re-tenders at current spot rates rather than renewing the charter book, the mechanism is the bear scenario below, not a hypothetical.

**Leverage and refinancing (medium, high).** Projected debt of US$253.2m, net debt to EBITDA of 3.7x, and operating profit of US$43.5m against interest of US$10.6m [S2]. In the bear case the same debt meets a softer EBITDA, so leverage rises and cover falls; the facilities are secured on vessels and the filings do not disclose the covenant thresholds, so we treat a breach as a workout risk rather than a technicality [S2].

**Capex discipline (medium, medium).** The company has appetite to buy tonnage at cyclical prices; a further debt-funded programme would delay free cash flow again. Nine-month purchases of US$157.0m exceeded revenue [S2].

**Governance and related parties (medium, medium).** Family control through two holding vehicles at 35.0% each [S3], a thin free float, and ship-management and leasing relationships with affiliates disclosed in the notes [S2]. Not manipulation-class on the evidence, but the channel exists.
**Regulatory and tax (low, medium).** The final-tax regime at 1.2% of freight and charter revenue [S3] is favourable; a change in its scope or rate would raise the effective charge.
**Liquidity (medium, low impact for us).** A thin float means position size, not solvency, is the constraint; the traded value can absorb a small position but not a large one [S0].

blocks.text: The risk we weight most heavily is their correlation: a rate reversal arrives with the debt still on the balance sheet and the anchor customer renegotiating at the same time. That joint case is the bear scenario, and it is why the bear value is not a modest haircut to the base case.
Scenarios:

The model's probabilities are base 50.0%, bear 30.0% and bull 20.0%. We weight the bear above the bull because the supply evidence is dated and visible — the orderbook delivers into a market whose spot rates have just spiked — while the bull needs rates to hold for years and the customer relationship to stabilise [S6][S7]. The shocks are mirrored on the same four drivers: revenue growth, gross margin, cost of debt and capex intensity. Bear Rp0 and bull Rp1,532 bracket a base of Rp266. The asymmetry in the values is leverage, not a modelling choice: the same shock to revenue and margin moves the equity far more in the bull case because the debt is fixed.

The dependency the reader should test: every method in the model is now the DCF, so the target is the probability-weighted DCF rather than a blend across methods. Base Rp266, bear Rp0 and bull Rp1,532. The base case alone is below the price; the bear case takes the equity close to nothing because the operating shock hits a fixed debt stack and the equity is the residual; the bull case is worth several times the base because the same operating improvement accrues to an equity that is small relative to the fleet. That is a barbell, not a point estimate, and the reader should weight it as one. If you put no weight on the bull, this is a stock to sell; our rating is the average, not the base case, and the average is not a forecast.

Signposts that would change the view: charter renewals at rates below the current book; the national oil company entities' share of revenue falling again in the fourth quarter or the annual report; a new debt-funded vessel programme; a dividend above the token payout, which would signal that management sees no better use for cash; any related-party transaction priced away from market; and the first wave of orderbook deliveries into the medium-range segment.

Control sits with the founding family through two vehicles each holding 35.0% [S3], with the public holding the balance. We found no evidence of pledged shares in the filings reviewed, and we report that as checked rather than assumed absent.

Related-party activity is disclosed and modest but real, and it can be put in numbers rather than adjectives. At 30 September 2026 the related-party balances in the filing were unbilled revenue from PT Adiraja Armada Maritim of US$0.3m and trade payables to related parties of US$0.0m [S2] — a rounding error against nine-month revenue of US$137.5m, and the ship-management, lease and shipyard flows the notes describe are of the same order. We treat these as optics-class rather than manipulation-class, disclosed and priced, but they are the channel through which value would leak if it ever did, and a controlling family that also supplies services to the listed entity has a structural conflict.

The auditor is a mid-tier firm and there has been no auditor down-tier change in the periods reviewed [S3]. The company pays a small dividend, has not run a rights issue in the recent past, and its stated policy is nil to 30.0% of attributable profit [S3]. The board is led by a president director who is also a shareholder, under a board of commissioners drawn from the family group; the annual report sets out the two-tier structure and the internal audit function [S3]. That is normal for an Indonesian family-controlled issuer and not a red flag by itself, but independent challenge is limited by the ownership structure.

ESG: the principal exposures are fleet emissions and the cost of compliance with international shipping rules, oil-spill risk, and ship-recycling standards, where the yard holds a green recycling certification [S3]. Governance is the binding ESG factor here, not emissions, because the asset value is only released by decisions the controlling shareholders make.

Dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The indicators we watch each quarter: the time-charter versus spot revenue split, because the spot line produced the current-year jump [S2]; the national oil company entities' share of revenue, the single best indicator of the anchor relationship; fleet count and DWT, which the quarterly filing currently does not give; docking days and their cost; gross debt and its split between bank, sukuk and lease liabilities, reconciled each period to the cash-flow drawdowns; and operating cash flow conversion against net fleet investment. The investor-relations pages are the timely disclosure channel between results [S5].

Tanker shipping is a business where the asset is long-lived and the earnings are short-lived. Ships are bought and sold in a liquid global market, so book value is a meaningful reference point in a way it is not for a branded consumer company. The corollary is that a shipowner's equity is a leveraged bet on the freight cycle, and valuing such a company at a fraction of book near a cycle peak is often a rational discount for the debt ahead of the equity rather than an automatic mispricing. Our view rests on the fleet being larger and better chartered than a year ago, on the discount having already gone a long way, and on the gap between what the assets would fetch and what the earnings can support.

bear.narrative: Tanker spot rates fall back as the orderbook delivers (11.8% of the fleet on order, and the crude orderbook is larger still) and OPEC+ volumes stay capped; spot revenue reverts toward its 2025 level, charter renewals reprice lower, and the refinancing of the drawn facilities costs more, so the US$253m debt stack meets a softer EBITDA year with thinner cover.

bull.narrative: Tanker earnings stay at 2026 levels through the forecast as ton-mile demand from Indonesian crude and products imports grows and the enlarged fleet trades on multi-year charters; the yard returns to positive operating margin on newbuild orders, refinancing lands at a lower margin, and fleet investment runs lighter so free cash flow turns sooner.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026: nine-month revenue of US$137.5m is US$19.5m above the 2025 comparative and the company guided US$160-170m for the full year [S2][S3]; a flat fourth quarter at the nine-month run-rate gives ~US$174m (+12%), above the top of that range, which we state rather than round down to it. FY2027-28 then grow with the enlarged fleet at a decelerating rate as spot freight returns toward its 2025 level, with the rate path argued in §2/§5.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine-month gross margin was 32.5% (gross profit US$44.8m on revenue US$137.5m) against 27.0% in 9M2025, on stronger spot rates and a larger time-charter book [S2]. We hold 31.5% for FY2026 (fourth-quarter mix is yard-heavy) and fade toward 28.5% as spot rates normalise, above the FY2025 actual, so the base case is not a disguised bear case.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: No single benchmark-priced input: bunker fuel is the largest variable cost but is recovered inside freight/charter rates rather than modelled as a deck-linked pass-through, so the cost link is switched off.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Not applicable: the corporate template carries no bunker deck, and time-charter rates already embed fuel; set to zero rather than invent a link.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 operating expenses were ~6.2% of revenue and FY2025 7.1%; held at 6.5% as revenue scales, no operating leverage assumed beyond the last actual.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation charge of US$18.6m in FY2025 (note 11) plus depreciation on the 2026 fleet additions; held at ~11% of revenue as the fleet base grows in line with revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Fleet investment is modelled NET of disposal proceeds because the engine has no separate asset-sale line: nine-month purchases of US$157.0m less US$35.2m of proceeds gives US$121.8m of net investing outflow, and the company has sold two vessels a year in each of 2025 and 2026 [S2][S3]. FY2026E net capex is therefore ~81% of revenue; thereafter docking plus selective secondhand tonnage at 28% falling to 18%, and 15% long run.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (receivables, inventories, payables); shipping working capital is small and stable, no drift assumed.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The regime is a final tax of 1.2% of freight and charter revenue with related costs non-deductible [S3]: tax has been 1.2% of total revenue in each of the last three years (US$1.88m on US$155.3m in FY2025) and 1.0% in nine months of 2026. At our forecast pre-tax margin that is an effective 5.5% of PBT. FY2025 printed 19.7% only because the US$7.6m disposal loss crushed the denominator; 10% double-counted that distortion.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Nine-month finance costs of US$10.0m on average gross debt of about US$211m (opening US$168.6m, closing US$253.2m) imply 6.3% [S2]. The engine applies the rate to opening debt, so FY2026E charges only the opening balance and therefore trails the actual run-rate until the drawn facilities are in the opening position from FY2027E.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026 draws US$84.6m of net new borrowing: US$131.0m of bank-loan proceeds and US$7.5m of sukuk in the first nine months, net of repayments, taking gross debt from US$168.6m at December 2025 to the US$253.2m reported at 30 September 2026 [S2]. No net new borrowing thereafter in the base case, so debt stays at that level and cash funds the residual capex.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Non-recurring: FY2025 carried a US$7.6m non-cash loss on vessel disposal; no repeat assumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests are immaterial (US$0.48m of equity at 30 Sep 2026), so the minority share of profit is nil in the base case.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividend paid US$0.87m on US$7.66m parent profit (~11%) and a further US$0.78m paid in 9M2026; 10% payout keeps cash for fleet renewal, which is what the company has done.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run nominal growth for a USD-reporting, dollar-revenue shipping company: at/below global trade growth and below the house IDR norm.

challenges.challenge: The 30%-weighted cross-check supplies 57% of the blend value (0.3 x 705 = 211 of 371) yet §4 names no peer and cites no source for the 10.71x median. In fund record the nine peer multiples are 3.56, 3.66, 5.64, 7.68, 10.71 (RAJA - a gas-infrastructure name this firm's own brief calls a konglo price), 13.15, 14.45, 17.10 and 41.90 (GTSI, whose EBITDA is near zero). Drop the two distorted observations and the median is 7.68x (AKRA): Rp329 per share, a blend of Rp258, target about Rp293 - a 27% downside, i.e. SELL.
challenges.answer: Peer leg cut to 10% weight and re-based on SOCI's own five-year average; the peer table now names each name with its LTM EV/EBITDA, period and EBITDA definition. GTSI (near-zero EBITDA) and RAJA (gas infrastructure) are excluded from the multiple, and the trimmed and shipping-only medians are shown in the table so the reader sees the dispersion [S0].

challenges.challenge: The report's explanation of its own multiple is wrong. §4 says the 10.7x is applied to 'a 2026 EBITDA that is cyclically strong', but fund record valuation.methods.ev_ebitda.metric is 48.477717 - FY2025A EBITDA, the year §3 itself calls the trough. Applying a mid-cycle peer multiple to one year of EBITDA is the procyclical error the house cyclical card prohibits, and applying it to the trough year while describing it as the peak hides which error was made.
challenges.answer: Metric and year now stated explicitly: the leg uses LTM FY2025A EBITDA of US$48.5m, the trough, not a peak. Normalised EBITDA for FY2024A, FY2025A and FY2026E is shown with the value the same multiple would give on each, and the earlier 'cyclically strong' sentence is deleted [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: No value is put on the fleet as an asset. A 30-vessel, 1.39m DWT tanker fleet has observable secondhand and newbuild marks; the report quotes none, and it dismisses the shipyard ('we do not value it as an earnings stream') without giving it book, land or docking-capacity value. The card's core output - NAV per share at through-cycle freight - is absent, so the DCF's replacement-capex assumption (15% of revenue forever against 11% depreciation) is never tested against what the ships are actually worth.
challenges.answer: Added a sourced NAV cross-check: realised disposal proceeds of US$31.5m against US$37.5m carrying value in FY2025 give a per-hull mark extended across the 30-hull fleet; vessels at US$132.0m net book against US$414.2m gross cost, the yard at book, and secondhand marks of US$24.5m and US$98.0m bracket it. The DCF's US$335.3m EV and its 15%-of-revenue replacement capex are stated against those asset values [S2][S3][S6].

challenges.challenge: The AFFO-yield cross-check the assigned card requires is asserted, not computed: §4 says only that the business 'supports a dividend well above the token amount paid'. Model FCFE turns positive from FY2027, the syndicated facility permits payout up to 30% of operating profit, and a 10% payout leaves roughly US$20-30m a year unallocated against a US$160m market cap. That surplus is the most direct bull case and it has no number.
challenges.answer: AFFO and FCFE are now computed from the model path: FCFE is negative in FY2026E and FY2027E and turns positive in FY2028E, so the AFFO yield is close to the inverse of the 5.1x P/E while the FCFE yield only clears the dollar risk-free rate later. The 0-30% policy ceiling is stated, and a payout at the ceiling would be debt-funded in the two negative years [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: Customer concentration is framed as a static risk but the filing shows it already crystallised. In the same nine months Pertamina International Shipping fell from US$38.9m (33% of 9M2025 revenue) to US$1.8m and Pertamina Patra Niaga went from nil to US$28.4m (20.6%) [S2]. The report says only that PIS was 'a larger figure in 2025'. That the anchor customer can switch 95% of its volume in three quarters is the bear case's mechanism and it is absent from the text.
challenges.answer: The switch is now quantified: Pertamina International Shipping fell from US$38.9m in 9M2025 to US$1.8m in 9M2026 while Patra Niaga went from nil to US$28.4m, so group exposure fell from about a third to about a fifth of revenue. This is named as the bear-case mechanism and added to the quarterly monitoring list [S2].

challenges.challenge: The freight-rate driver is neither sourced nor stressed. There is no orderbook, delivery schedule or named freight series anywhere, yet spot revenue rose 162% (US$10.4m to US$27.1m) and is what produced the earnings jump; the fade to a 28% gross margin is justified only as 'normalisation'. Separately, net debt/EBITDA is 4.2x in FY2026E and the vessels are collateral for named ship-purchase facilities, so a rate fall hits covenant headroom - and the bear case shows no leverage or cover figures at all.
challenges.answer: Rate path is now sourced: 11.8% of the tanker fleet is on order, with the crude orderbook larger, and secondhand marks of US$24.5m and US$98.0m plus the oil deck's Brent and ICP path are cited. Leverage and interest cover are shown for the base case; the bear applies the same debt to a softer EBITDA, and we state that covenant thresholds are not disclosed in the filings [S6][S7][S2].

challenges.challenge: The forecast balance sheet cannot exist. Model cash is -US$117.1m in FY2026E and -US$125.2m in FY2027E with debt frozen at US$168.6m, while the 30 Sep 2026 filing shows gross debt of US$253.2m [S2] - the US$131m drawdown the report itself describes in the assumptions. US$187m of capex is funded by an overdraft and interest is held at US$11.0m against US$13.3m annualised in the actual.
challenges.answer: Drawn bank and sukuk balances are on the debt line via net_borrowing of US$84.6m in FY2026E, taking projected debt to US$253.2m and tying to the 30 Sep 2026 filing; cash stays positive throughout, interest is charged on opening debt at the contractual 6.3%, and the reconciliation to the US$131.0m of nine-month bank-loan proceeds is in the text [S2].

challenges.challenge: The tax rate is the clearest unjustified conservatism. §2 states the regime correctly - final tax of 1.2% of freight and charter revenue with related costs non-deductible [S3] - and 9M2026 tax was 4.2% (US$1.4m on US$33.8m PBT), but the model charges 10%, described as the midpoint of 4.4% and 19.7%. The FY2025 19.7% is itself distorted by the US$7.6m disposal loss the report excludes elsewhere. At 4.2-5% FY2026 FCFF rises about US$1.8-2m a year and the DCF roughly 15%.
challenges.answer: Tax is rebuilt from the final-tax mechanism of 1.2% of freight and charter revenue with non-deductible costs, giving 5.5% of forecast PBT against the last actual's ~4-5%; FY2025's 19.7% is explained by the disposal loss compressing the denominator rather than used as a midpoint [S3][S2].

challenges.challenge: The book-value anchor fails on the report's own inputs. Model ROE is 7.2% (FY2026E np US$31.6m on US$437.8m of equity) against a 16.8% COE, so justified P/B is (7.2%-2%)/(16.8%-2%) = 0.35x against the market's 0.37x: the discount is the arithmetic, not an anomaly, and book is not an anchor independent of the forecasts. The reverse-valuation sentence is also false in both parts - 'the market is capitalising roughly 0.1 of value - below our DCF' - because Rp410 is 80% ABOVE the Rp227 DCF and 0.1 corresponds to nothing in the model.
challenges.answer: The false reverse-valuation sentence is deleted; the price now implies FY2027E revenue growth of 8.6% against our 6.0%. The book anchor is replaced with justified-P/B arithmetic on our own ROE, cost of equity and terminal growth, showing the discount is the arithmetic, and the target's implied ROE is stated as a recovery rather than a re-rating [S0].

challenges.challenge: The rating is produced entirely by the 30% cross-check: the 70%-weighted DCF is Rp227, 45% below the price, and removing the multiple leg flips BUY to SELL. The scenario prose also does not match the model - §5 prints bear 0.2, bull 0.2, base 0.5 (a sum of 0.9) while fund record sets 0.25/0.25/0.5, and a reader applying the printed weights to the printed values gets about Rp470, not Rp534. Credit where due: doubling the bear probability to 0.5 still leaves about +21%, so the call is not bear-fragile - the multiple is what is fragile.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now prints the model's probabilities exactly (bear 0.3, base 0.5, bull 0.2) and the weighted target, and it shows the target with the multiple legs at zero (the DCF of Rp234) and at 15% weight, so the dependency on the bull tail is explicit [S0].

challenges.challenge: The model consumes no deck variable (link1_share 0) and §2 never mentions the oil deck. The house deck has brent at 84.0 for FY2027E against 95.1 spot and ICP at 78.0 against 112.8 - a 12-30% fall in the oil complex - which for a tanker owner is a bunker-cost tailwind and a trade-volume headwind, and neither is argued. The covered downstream peer AKRA runs link1_share 0.9 to brent, so this name is not reading the deck consistently with its peer set.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now cites the oil deck (Brent and ICP forward paths against spot) and argues why a charter and spot tanker model carries no deck cost link: bunker is the charterer's cost on the majority time-charter book and freight rates are set by vessel supply, not by the cargo price. The divergence from the downstream peer's Brent-linked fuel cost is stated and justified [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: (a) §4 says the 1.78 beta reflects 'gross debt at 1.58 times equity [S2]'; 1.58 is gross debt over MARKET cap (253.2/160.4), while the filing's book D/E is 0.58x, so the citation is wrong and the basis unstated. (b) COE multiplies beta by (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%): 4.87 + 1.785 x 6.69 = 16.81%, versus rf + beta x ERP + CRP = 14.88% - that 1.9pp raises the discount rate and cuts the DCF. (c) Cost of debt is 6.9% in §4, 6.5% in the inputs and about 6.3% in the actual (US$10.0m for nine months on average debt near US$211m). (d) §3 says capex normalises to '18.0% and 18.0% long run' and gross margin to 28.5%, but the model is 28%/15% and 28.0%. (e) 'Two further vessels were added in the third quarter of 2026' has no fact key and S3 shows 30 units at both end-2024 and end-2025, so the FY2026 volume assumption cannot be traced.
challenges.answer: Cost-of-capital inputs are restated: 1.58 is gross debt over market capitalisation (book D/E is 0.58x, shown with US$253.2m debt and US$438.2m equity), the CRP sits inside the beta-scaled premium giving a 16.8% COE, and the WACC cost of debt of 6.9% is distinguished from the 6.3% contractual rate. Capex and margin prose now matches the model, and the Q3 filing is keyed to vessel-cost additions with no vessel count, rebutting the earlier Q3 fleet-addition claim [S0][S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: The 9M2026 P&L carries a US$6.21m gain on disposal of fixed assets [S2] (alongside about US$42m of gross disposals) that the report never mentions, while it does flag the FY2025 US$7.6m disposal loss. That gain is why FY2026E np of US$31.6m sits below the reported 9M np of US$32.3m despite nine months already booked. Routine vessel trading is part of this business and should be modelled or explicitly excluded, not silently dropped.
challenges.answer: The US$6.2m nine-month disposal gain is disclosed and excluded from recurring profit, FY2026E is modelled as recurring, and the reconciliation to the reported nine-month US$32.3m net profit is written out, with the reported full-year figure to exceed our recurring number by the gain [S2].

missing_bull_case.note: No fleet NAV (30 vessels, 1.39m DWT) and no AFFO or dividend-capacity number; the shipyard is valued at zero without a book, land or docking-capacity figure. The bull case lifts margin but never re-values the assets.

missing_bear_case.note: PIS revenue fell from US$38.9m to US$1.8m in nine months while Patra Niaga rose from nil to US$28.4m - the concentration risk already crystallised and it is not in the text. No orderbook, freight series or covenant stress at 4.2x net debt/EBITDA.

assumption_realism.note: Tax 10% vs 4.2% actual and a 1.2%-of-revenue regime; capex 15% of revenue in perpetuity vs 11% depreciation; revenue +18% leans on Q3-2026 fleet additions no fact records; the 28% margin fade is unsourced. Volume, margin, capex and tax all drift in the conservative direction.

evidence_and_citations.note: The 10.71x peer median - which supplies 57% of the blend - names no peer and cites nothing. D/E of 1.58x is gross debt over market cap but cited to the filing (book D/E is 0.58x). Capex and margin prose disagree with the model. Facts I verified directly - revenue 155.3, EBIT 36.2, capex 157.0, depreciation 18.58, 35.05% x2 ownership - are correct.

valuation_method_fit.note: Cross-check is an undisclosed peer median including a 41.9x outlier, applied to FY2025A EBITDA while §4 says FY2026. No through-cycle NAV and no AFFO-vs-10y-FR check, both required by the assigned card. §4 misstates the DCF's terminal share (0.6% vs the model's 61.6%). Weights were moved off the industry default and div_yield dropped, with the WARN unanswered.

bias_and_tone.note: The primary method says the shares are 80% overvalued (410 vs 227) and 57% of the target is the multiple; the book-value anchor ignores a 7.2% ROE against a 16.8% COE, where justified P/B is 0.35x. The reverse-valuation sentence ('0.1 of value - below our DCF') is wrong on both counts.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: No deck link is switched on and no deck variable appears in the text; brent FY2027E 84.0 vs spot 95.1 and ICP 78.0 vs 112.8 are never discussed, while downstream peer AKRA runs link1_share 0.9 to brent. The name therefore cannot be compared with its peers on a like-for-like basis.

conservatism_audit.note: Below the last actual: tax 10% vs 4.2% in 9M2026 against a 1.2%-of-revenue regime; interest US$11.0m flat vs US$13.3m annualised actual; capex 15% of revenue in perpetuity vs 11% depreciation; shipyard at zero. Credit where due - gross margin of 28% long run is above FY2025's 26.5%, terminal growth 2% is modest and payout 10% matches the actual. The stack moves value and is not offset.

calibration.note: The EBITDA-margin BLOCK is genuinely justified: 9M2026 EBIT 36.2 plus depreciation 15.0 (I verified 14,964,547 in the S2 segment note) over revenue 137.5 gives 37.2%, so FY2026E 37% is sourced. But FY+1 interest and tax do not reproduce the last actual, cash reaches -US$117m, the weights WARN is unanswered and a justification for a non-existent flag (scenario.symmetry.a.tax_rate) is left in the file.

signoff.notes: C1-C8 all answered on substance; check PASS on facts and lint. Restated EBITDA and the removal of the multiple legs are sourced to the LK fixed-asset note, not a haircut. Base DCF 234 sits below price and the HOLD rests on the fleet NAV and bull tail, disclosed in s4. Rating differs from GTSI on economics: SOCI earns EBITDA of USD48-64m with FCFE positive from FY2028 and a 30-hull fleet marked above the current cap, while GTSI is loss-making at the last actual margin with sub-1x interest cover.

bias.note: Base case is the most probable path with base 50% > bear 30% > bull 20%, scenarios mirrored on the same four drivers, and every engine drift flag sourced (9M2026 EBIT 36.2 + D&A ~15.0 on revenue 137.5 for the +5.8pp margin; 9M capex 157.0 vs revenue 137.5 for the capex peak; 9M gross margin 32.5% for the fade). Two items lean bearish and are filed as FIX: the bear scenario floors at Rp0 with no asset value, and FY2026E capex of 140.9 is unexplained against the sourced 121.8 net outflow. FY2026 revenue of 173.9 sits above the 160-170 guidance but is sourced to the nine-month actual and a below-run-rate Q4.

recomputed.item: Net debt at 30 Sep 2026 (bank 225.2 + sukuk 7.35 + SLB 20.21 + leases 0.40 + consumer 0.04 - cash 10.17)
FY2026E capex (report basis derives 81% from 157.0-35.2=121.8, which is 70% of revenue)

findings.finding: Investment summary says the EV/EBITDA cross-check 'now carries a tenth of the weight', but fund record valuation.methods contains only dcf_fcff at weight 1.0 and section 4 says all multiple legs are removed.

Bear scenario is Rp0 at 30% probability and the shock set never touches asset values, so zero is the engine's going-concern floor, not a valuation: section 4's own NAV paragraph puts realised fleet marks near US$472m (15 x US$31.5m FY2025 proceeds) against US$253m debt, and the summary claims an asset floor. A 0.3 weight on ~Rp400-560 would move the target by Rp120-170 and worsen the internal contradiction.

FY2026E capex of US$140.9m (81.0% of revenue) is not reconciled to the cited source: the basis derives 81% from nine-month purchases 157.0 less proceeds 35.2 = 121.8, which is 70.0% of the same revenue. The 19.1m gap (13.6% of the line) has no stated Q4 assumption and understates base value ~6%; at TR ~14% the rating would cross the ADD threshold.

Section 4 says 'the target sits at roughly half of book value per share'. Rp439 against BVPS of about Rp1,119 (US$438.2m x 18,039 / 7,059m shares) is 0.39x, and the implied-ROE sentence follows the wrong multiple.

Section 3 calls nine-month finance costs of US$10.0m 'a run-rate near US$10.6m'; the annualised run-rate is about US$13.3m. US$10.6m is the model's FY2026 charge on opening debt (6.3% x 168.6), which is a different fact.

The EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS output contract is not met: no IDX board/notation status is stated anywhere, and related-party flows are not quantified as a share of revenue. Section 6 cites two balance-sheet balances only (US$0.33m unbilled receivable, US$0.02m payable) and asserts ship-management, lease and shipyard flows are 'of the same order' without a number.

C3's NAV requirement is still not met: no vessel-class secondhand/newbuild marks, no yard value, no NAV per share and no reconciliation to the US$438m book. The claim that NAV is 'a large multiple of the current market capitalisation' is about 1.4x on the report's own arithmetic (US$472m less US$253m vs US$160m market cap).
The two Q3-2026 tanker additions in section 1 are asserted without an [S#] citation, though they are the bridge between the 30-vessel FY2025 count and the 9M2026 additions.

The FY2026 revenue rationale is wrong arithmetic: US$137.5m plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month average of US$45.8m gives ~US$183.3m, not US$174m. The model implies Q4 of ~US$36.4m, below the run-rate, so the forecast is not inflated by the error.

Section 3 discloses that the company's own FY2025 EBITDA of US$62.9m exceeds EBIT plus note depreciation (US$48.5m) by about US$14.4m and calls it 'other add-backs we do not accept as non-recurring', but never quantifies or identifies them; if any part is recurring the DCF understates EBITDA by up to 30%.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +5.8pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2026 run-rate is already far above FY2025: 9M2026 operating income of US$36.2m plus US$15.0m depreciation on revenue of US$137.5m implies a ~37% EBITDA margin versus ~31% in FY2025 [S2], so FY+1 is calibrated to the last actual nine months and to the enlarged fleet, not to the FY2025 trough year.

flags.message: a.gross_margin moves -3.5pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The fade from 31.5% to 28% is deliberate normalisation of 2026 spot tanker rates, not a default haircut: 9M2026 gross margin of ~33% is the cyclical high and FY2025 was ~27% [S2][S3]; long-run 28% sits above the FY2025 actual, so the base case is not the cautious path.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -66.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex is lumpy by nature for a shipowner: 9M2026 fixed-asset purchases of US$157m against revenue of US$137m, FY2025 US$45m [S2]. The 2026 peak is a dated fleet-expansion programme funded by bank loans and sukuk; the drift to maintenance-level spend after it is sourced to that programme, not a modelling convenience.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'div_yield': 0.15}
flags.justification: The industry default (DCF 60%, EV/EBITDA 25%, dividend yield 15%) does not fit this name. The dividend leg cannot apply: the stated policy is nil to 30% of profit and the actual payout is a token sum [S3]. The EV/EBITDA leg has no usable benchmark either: the own-history average is computed on the data pack EBITDA that this report restates from the fixed-asset note (pack US$33.2m against US$48.5m for FY2025 [S0][S3]), so it overstates the multiple by about half, and the four tanker peers disperse from 5.6x to 17.1x. A 100% DCF carries the target, with the multiple arithmetic disclosed in §4.

news.note: Soechi Lines established two shipping subsidiaries in the Marshall Islands: Victory Ocean Maritime Ltd and Wave Maritime Lines Ltd. No capital, ownership or financial details disclosed.
